Video of a robot I'm building

Here's another video of the robot going through some of his motions the delays taken out.

For the past couple of months I've been working on a hexapod robot. I'm calling him Twitchy. He's currently powered by a 2200mAh LiPo battery. I'm using an Arduino as the microcontroller, and a couple of servo controller boards from Adafruit. I have a 2A buck converter powering the Arduino through the barrel jack, and a 12A buck converter powering the servos using 6V. Twitchy is a work in progress, and I'll be adding more hardware to him from time to time. I'm going to be adding a voltage regulator to keep me from draining the battery too much, and a 15A circuit breaker to keep me from damaging my electronic components due to a short. I'm also planning on adding a Beagle Bone Black with a Wifi dongle, or an Arduino Wifi shield, to allow me to control my robot from my computer over my home network I eventually plan on also adding some sensors, and hopefully a small web cam in the future.

Nice work. I feel like you could improve the speed significantly if you worked the leg rotation in while only 3 feet were on the ground pushing backwards while the feet in the air moved forward.

Also it seems like the servos are not rotating as much as I might expect. Was this intentional?

That's an idea I'll have to consider. I have the rotations on the servos limited to keep it standing properly. I've found that if I don't keep the legs spread out enough it tends to tip to the side. Since I've never worked on a walking robot before it's a lot of trial an error to get him moving reliably.

I haven't ventured into making a walking robot myself yet. But you are making me want to try. I wouldn't call myself an expert but I have a few more ideas for you.

A pid loop on the leg movement might help with the smoothness and stability.

Using a smaller battery might make balancing easier.

If you sacrifice some ground clearance putting the last leg segment at a slightly flatter angle would increase your stance a bit as well.

The servos don't support PID functionality so that's not an option. If I get creative with small tilt sensors then I could get some feedback from the legs. The real question with that approach would be how much crazier I want to get with the wiring. The jerky movement of the servos is mainly being caused by the speed that they're moving. I can tell each servo to go to a specific angle, and it'll go there as fast as it can then stop immediately. I could get smoother movement by slowing them down. That would involve telling them to move in smaller increments. I'm already using the smallest battery I can find that will do the job. It's near the bottom of the robot, and lowers the center of gravity quite a bit. The ground clearance is a trade off. The lower to the ground it is the more stable it will be, but the that will also make it harder to get over obstacles without programming designed to specifically lift the legs over the obstacle. I'm only on the first draft of the software, and it'll be improved upon with time. Right now I'm in the process of figuring out the basest series of movements that are required to perform a specific action. Once I have the basics down I'll be going back over my library, and creating a better version. I'm eventually wanting to add an ultrasonic range finder to allow it to determine how far away from something it is, and I've been thinking about putting a few tilt sensors on the body. At this point the main limitation is going to be figuring out how to cram all of the hardware I want onto such a small chassis. I was originally wanting to put all of the electronics inside of it, but that proved to be impossible.

Program the pid loop into your code. Feed the smoothed value to the servo just the same. This solves the exact problem you describe. I will try and find the example that made it make sense to me. I've used it on camera mounts and arms before.

Found it. http://lab.guilhermemartins.net/2009/08/21/filtering-servo-movements/

If you want to incorporate a tilt sensor just one on the body would do. Then adjust leg position to keep the body level. That starts to get really difficult fast though.

For some reason I was thinking that would require feedback from the servo about the position. I'll do some more reading on the subject in the future. From what I gather, the gist of it is to slow the servo movement as it approaches it's destination angle so it doesn't come to a hard start. I haven't had a moment to really look it over. It's an idea that I'll consider. A lot of the math in my programming is off, and I need to put the robot through some more positioning tests to determine my actual maximum and minimum values for the servo positions.

One will do, but that'd only allow me to detect a tilt on one plane. If I decide to do that then I'll want to use at least two so I can level it in both directions.

I think the next thing I'll want to look into will be getting some multithreading going on the Arduino. At the moment I'm using the delay() function to pause the servos in between movements, and that approach simply won't be useful when I start adding sensors on to Twitchy. After that I'll be looking into getting a Beagle Bone Black and WiFi dongle added. I'm probably going to need to redo a lot of my electronics package to fit more components on board. I'm hoping that I'll just need to add another mounting plate to hold the additional components at this point.

Exactly. You will have to ditch the delay for the pid loop to function correctly. But then your starts and stops will be much smoother.

For finding the values for your pwm I like to use a pot and echo the value out on serial, I have noticed different servos like different values and frequencies.

Also, there are triple axis sensors that can tell you everything about the orientation of your body with one unit.

I look forward to seeing twitchy progress.
